pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Newton's Third Law

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** The UK KS3 national curriculum frames forces as 'arising from the interaction between 2 objects' and covers 'opposing forces and equilibrium' but names the laws explicitly only at KS4.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** NGSS MS-PS2-1 ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-1]', limited to 1-D vertical/horizontal interactions; engineering-integrated); DCI PS2.A states the equal-and-opposite pair for interacting objects.

- **Operational details:** At 12-13 pupils meet Newton's Third Law: for any pair of interacting objects, the force A exerts on B is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force B exerts on A — and crucially these two forces act on DIFFERENT bodies. This is the hardest of the three laws (one two-tier study found ~68.5% holding a misconception, and performance is reliably worse in gravitational than in contact contexts).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal-operational/quantitative). The key cognitive move at this age is to identify the TWO bodies in the interaction and resist treating the pair as forces on one object that 'cancel'. Frame the law as a single INTERACTION between two bodies (A on B, B on A) rather than 'action then reaction' — the action/reaction wording implies a false time sequence and drives the same-body error (IOP; Taber).
bestPractices: Frame the law as a single INTERACTION between two bodies (A on B, B on A), not sequential 'action then reaction' — the words imply a false time order and feed the same-body error (IOP; Taber)

Teach the three diagnostic features of a true pair: they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies, are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, and are the SAME type of force (both gravitational, or both contact)

Explicitly contrast a third-law pair with balanced forces on ONE body — book on a table: weight + table's push both act on the book (balanced, NOT a pair); the partner to the book's weight is the book's gravitational pull on the Earth
Use kinaesthetic demos so students FEEL both bodies get a force (trolleys, skateboards, metre-rule pull; back-to-back force-meters that stay equal even during acceleration)
Deliberately address the gravity-context version (performance is worse there) as well as contact pushes
Resolve 'the bigger/active object pushes harder' with equal-force/different-effect cases (bug & windscreen; different accelerations come from different masses via N2)
keyRepresentations: Two separate free-body diagrams side by side, one per body, each showing its half of the pair on a different object
The 'swap and reverse' test (A↔B) to locate the partner force
Book / table / Earth three-bodies diagram separating the interaction pairs from the balanced forces on the book
commonMisconceptions: Pairing the two forces on the SAME body and concluding they cancel — conflating a third-law pair with balanced forces (the central error; Taber)
During acceleration the 'active' pusher exerts the bigger force ('Blue pushes Green harder to start the motion') — reported in ~100% of incoming students and very stubborn
The more massive object exerts more force (forces are equal; different EFFECTS come from different masses)
'Action' then 'reaction' implies a time sequence (B responds after A), rather than simultaneous forces
Third-law forces 'cancel out' (they act on different bodies, so can never cancel on one body)
Greater difficulty identifying the partner force in gravitational interactions than in contact pushes

learn.summary: Newton's Third Law for ages 12–13: every force is one half of an interaction between TWO objects — if A pushes or pulls B, then B pushes or pulls A with an equal-magnitude, opposite-direction force of the same type. The decisive learner moves are to name the two different bodies in each pair, to see the pair stays equal even during acceleration and for very different masses, and to distinguish a third-law pair (two bodies) from balanced forces on one body. This is the hardest of Newton's laws; the central misconception is fusing a third-law pair with balanced forces on a single object and concluding they 'cancel'. Frame the law as one simultaneous interaction, not sequential 'action then reaction'.

activities.title: Matched force-meters: the pair stays equal
feedback: If you predicted the harder/active pusher's meter reads more: look again — the readings stay matched even as you push harder and even while the carts speed up together. The interaction force on each object is equal.

Name the object each reading belongs to: the measured interaction force acts on cart A one way and on cart B the opposite way — one force per object. Because they act on different objects they form a genuine third-law pair, not two forces on one body.

A static picture can show the two arrows, but watching the readings stay equal while you push harder is what directly tests the 'active object pushes harder' idea; if you only have a diagram, reason explicitly about what the sensors would read during acceleration. Any small difference between real readings comes from instrument limitations (precision, zeroing or calibration, or the sensors' own mass while accelerating). The interaction pair is equal in principle, and friction with the ground is a separate force that does NOT make the two readings unequal.
activities.rationale: The 'active/bigger object pushes harder during acceleration' idea is reported as common and stubborn; a live, equal-reading measurement during acceleration lets learners confront it directly. A prediction-first step surfaces the misconception before the evidence.
sourceClaims: Third-law pairs act on two different bodies, are equal and opposite, and are the same type of force; they do NOT cancel (each acts on a different body). 'Action/reaction' is misleading. Book-on-table involves three bodies (Earth, book, table): the book's weight pairs with the book's pull on the Earth, and the book-on-table push pairs with the table-on-book push — while the two forces ON the book merely balance.
learnerActions: Set two carts nose-to-nose with a push–pull force sensor on the front of each, touching (ordinary spring newton-meters only measure pulls; if that is all you have, hook two together and have one cart tow the other instead), and predict, before pushing, what each sensor will read when one cart pushes gently and when it pushes hard.
Make one cart push the other and read both sensors; then push harder and read again; then keep pushing so both carts speed up together, and read the sensors while they are accelerating.
Record whether the two readings are ever different, including while the carts are speeding up.
State in your own words which object each measured force acts on.
activities.intendedInsight: The two forces in an interaction are always equal in magnitude, even while the objects accelerate and even when one is doing the 'pushing' — so there is no 'stronger pusher'.

activities.title: Find the partner: two bodies, never the same one
feedback: If you placed both forces of a 'pair' on the same object, re-run the swap test: the partner of 'skater pushes wall' is 'wall pushes skater' — a different object. The skater is pushed away from the wall, and the wall is pushed away from the skater (in the direction of the skater's push).
Because the two forces act on different bodies, they cannot add up or cancel on one body; cancelling only happens between forces on the SAME body.
Optional highlight tools make the partner's object obvious, but the key check is verbal: name both objects every time.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating the two bodies and using the 'B on A' locating rule targets the same-body/cancellation error identified as central. Framing it as one interaction (not action-then-reaction) avoids implying a time sequence.
sourceClaims: Third-law pairs act on two different bodies, are equal and opposite, and are the same type of force; they do NOT cancel (each acts on a different body). 'Action/reaction' is misleading. Book-on-table involves three bodies (Earth, book, table): the book's weight pairs with the book's pull on the Earth, and the book-on-table push pairs with the table-on-book push — while the two forces ON the book merely balance.

A common alternative conception is misidentifying the action/reaction pair as both acting on the same body and concluding they cancel; the law concerns forces on a pair of bodies and so cannot explain why forces on a single body balance. Careful language matters; framing force as a single interaction between two bodies helps.
learnerActions: Watch a skater shove a wall and recoil, or push off a wall yourself, and name the two forces: the force on the wall and the force on the skater.
For each named force, apply the 'swap and reverse' test: if 'A acts on B', its partner is 'B acts on A' — state it aloud.
Use a highlight tool (optional) that greys out everything except the partner force on the OTHER body, and check it lands on a different object.
Decide whether the two forces in a pair could ever cancel each other, and explain why or why not.
activities.intendedInsight: A third-law pair always consists of forces on two different objects, so the pair can never cancel on a single object.

activities.title: Equal forces, unequal effects (bug vs windscreen)
feedback: If you said the heavier or faster object exerts the bigger force: the forces are equal. The bug and the windscreen push on each other equally.
The difference you observe is in acceleration: for the same force, a smaller mass gives a larger acceleration (a = F/m).
Keep 'bigger force' and 'bigger effect' as two separate questions — conflating them is exactly the misconception.
activities.rationale: Resolving 'the bigger/more massive object pushes harder' with an equal-force/different-effect case links N3 to N2 and addresses a documented misconception without asserting new empirical efficacy.
sourceClaims: MS-PS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-1]' (examples: car collisions, meteor and space vehicle; assessment limited to 1-D vertical/horizontal interactions). DCI PS2.A: for any pair of interacting objects the force of the first on the second equals in strength the force of the second on the first, opposite in direction.
learnerActions: Consider a collision between a light object and a heavy object (e.g. a bug and a windscreen, or a small car and a truck); predict which experiences the bigger force.
Using a mass control (optional dial) or by reasoning, compare the forces on the two objects and then compare their accelerations.
Explain, using F = ma, why the lighter object changes its motion much more while the forces are equal.
Write one sentence separating 'which force is bigger' (neither — they're equal) from 'which object is affected more' (the lighter one).
activities.intendedInsight: Equal interaction forces produce different effects on different masses; the different accelerations come from the different masses (via F = ma), not from unequal forces (how much damage is done also depends on how fragile each object is).

activities.title: Book, table and Earth: pair vs balanced
feedback: If you called the table's push and the book's weight a pair: both act on the book, so they are balanced forces, not a pair.
The weight's partner is the book pulling the Earth up (both gravitational); the table-push's partner is the book pushing down on the table (both contact).
Use two checks for every candidate pair: different objects, and same type of force.
activities.rationale: The book/table/Earth case is the canonical setting where learners fuse balanced forces with a third-law pair; separating the interaction pairs from the one-body balance directly addresses the central error. A tap-to-reveal reference can support this, but a static version cannot show forces staying equal during acceleration, so pair it with the dynamic measurement activity.
sourceClaims: Third-law pairs act on two different bodies, are equal and opposite, and are the same type of force; they do NOT cancel (each acts on a different body). 'Action/reaction' is misleading. Book-on-table involves three bodies (Earth, book, table): the book's weight pairs with the book's pull on the Earth, and the book-on-table push pairs with the table-on-book push — while the two forces ON the book merely balance.

A common alternative conception is misidentifying the action/reaction pair as both acting on the same body and concluding they cancel; the law concerns forces on a pair of bodies and so cannot explain why forces on a single body balance. Careful language matters; framing force as a single interaction between two bodies helps.
learnerActions: Draw or reveal the three bodies in a book-on-table scene: Earth, book, table.
List the forces acting ON the book (its weight from the Earth, and the table's upward push) and state that these two balance because the book is at rest.
For the book's weight, find its third-law partner by the swap test (the book's gravitational pull up on the Earth).
For the table's push on the book, find its partner (the book's push down on the table).
Sort every named force into 'balanced forces on one body' versus 'third-law pair across two bodies', and check each pair is the same TYPE of force (both gravitational, or both contact).
activities.intendedInsight: The two forces on the book balance (same body) but are NOT a pair; each force's genuine partner acts on a different body and is the same type of force.

activities.title: Socratic 'am I pulling you?' questioning
feedback: If you described a delay or a sequence: the two forces happen at the same time — there is no first and second.
Notice you cannot pull the rule without it pulling back; the interaction is inherently two-sided.
Replacing 'action/reaction' with 'A on B / B on A' removes the false time-order cue.
activities.rationale: The questioning routine probes the simultaneity and mutuality of the interaction and supports language that avoids the sequence implication. It builds reasoning but does not provide the felt equality that a measured demonstration offers, so it complements rather than replaces the measurement activity.
sourceClaims: A common alternative conception is misidentifying the action/reaction pair as both acting on the same body and concluding they cancel; the law concerns forces on a pair of bodies and so cannot explain why forces on a single body balance. Careful language matters; framing force as a single interaction between two bodies helps.
learnerActions: With a partner or an in-role tutor, pull on opposite ends of a metre rule and answer: Which way am I pulling you? Which way are you pulling me?
Answer: Can I pull you without you pulling me back?
Relate your answers to the rule that the interaction is simultaneous — not 'my pull first, then your pull'.
Restate the law without using the words 'action' and 'reaction', using 'A on B' and 'B on A' instead.
activities.intendedInsight: Interaction forces are simultaneous and mutual; the 'action then reaction' wording wrongly implies a time order.

activities.title: Retrieval: sort pairs, match partners, apply
feedback: For any 'pair' you pick, confirm it passes both checks: two different objects AND the same type of force.
If you labelled two forces on one object a pair, they are balanced, not a pair.
For recoil, the gun pushes the bullet forward and the bullet pushes the gun back — equal forces, different objects.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorisation and applied items give retrieval practice and surface the same-body and 'pusher pushes harder' distractors. Recognition items assess discrimination but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and manipulate the interaction, so they are best used after the demonstration and reasoning activities.
sourceClaims: Third-law pairs act on two different bodies, are equal and opposite, and are the same type of force; they do NOT cancel (each acts on a different body). 'Action/reaction' is misleading. Book-on-table involves three bodies (Earth, book, table): the book's weight pairs with the book's pull on the Earth, and the book-on-table push pairs with the table-on-book push — while the two forces ON the book merely balance.
learnerActions: Match each named force to its partner on the OTHER body (e.g. 'rocket pushes gas down' ↔ 'gas pushes rocket up').
Categorise given force-pairs as 'third-law pair' or 'balanced forces on one body'.
Answer the book-on-table item: which forces form third-law pairs (there is more than one pair), and how do you decide?
For rocket propulsion and gun recoil, name both forces and the object each acts on.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can reliably identify third-law partners (different object, same type) and separate them from balanced forces across varied contexts.

constraints: Target age 12–13; this is the hardest of Newton's laws and the central misconception (fusing a third-law pair with balanced forces on one body) must be addressed explicitly, not assumed away.
Every third-law pair must satisfy two checks: the two forces act on DIFFERENT objects, and they are the SAME type of force (both gravitational, or both contact).
Avoid 'action then reaction' phrasing; use 'A on B' and 'B on A' to convey simultaneous, mutual forces.
Deliberately include a gravitational-context example (e.g. book/Earth), since learners find partner-finding harder there than in contact pushes.

Static tap-to-reveal diagrams are useful references but cannot show forces staying equal during acceleration; use them alongside, not instead of, a dynamic measurement that targets the 'active object pushes harder' idea.
Recognition/matching items assess discrimination but do not require independent construction of an interaction; follow them with tasks where learners name both objects and locate partners themselves.

Real newton-meters/force sensors are approximate instruments with limited precision; frame equal readings as evidence that the interaction forces are equal, treating any small difference as an instrument limitation (precision, zeroing/calibration, or the sensors' own mass during acceleration) rather than implying friction makes the pair unequal (friction is a separate force and does not affect the equality of the A-on-B / B-on-A pair).

NGSS MS-PS2-1 limits assessment to 1-D interactions; a planar treatment is sufficient and a 3-D representation adds handling cost without clear conceptual gain at this stage (a scoped observation, not a universal claim).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving these specific activities were tested.

The source cites a '~68.5% misconception' prevalence from a two-tier study and '~100% of incoming students' holding the 'active pusher pushes harder' idea; these figures are stated in the original pedagogy but are not attributed to a listed source[].claim, so they are reported here only as context, not as verified evidence, and are omitted from learner-facing text.

The Taber source (science-education-research.com) is marked verified:false in the row; claims drawn from it (language/framing, same-body cancellation error) are retained as pedagogical guidance but should be re-checked.

The original 'ideal' entry asserted the decisive facts 'do not survive a static treatment' and that a static image 'cannot' overturn the misconception; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, since catalog ratings do not establish such necessity claims.
The 3-D claim that it 'adds nothing' has been softened to a scoped observation tied to the 1-D standard and handling cost.

When describing collisions/recoil, note that equal forces coexist with different accelerations; any speeding-up/slowing description should reference the object's mass and initial motion rather than implying the resultant sets the current direction of travel.

Activity 1 was standardised to two linked newton-meters so the 'both meters read equal' comparison is coherent; the equal readings demonstrate the equal magnitude of the A-on-B and B-on-A interaction forces (treating the linking meter as approximately massless).

Corrected the measurement-limitation wording in Activity 1 feedback and the related constraint: third-law equality of the pair is exact, so any discrepancy in real readings is instrument precision/measurement noise; friction is a separate force and does not make the pair unequal. This avoids implying friction can unbalance a true third-law pair.

assess.poeTask: Hook two identical newton-meters (or force sensors) together and have two students pull — one gently, one hard. Ask the class to predict what each meter reads, and WHY, before they pull. Predicting the 'stronger' puller's meter reads more reveals the unequal-force idea; both reading the same, even during acceleration or with different-mass carts, is the surprise that establishes the equal pair.
probeDeeper: A truck and a small car collide head-on. Which experiences the bigger force — and why do they end up so differently damaged?
A rocket pushes hot gas downwards and rises. Name both forces in the pair and the object each one acts on.
For the two forces you called a pair — do they act on the same object or different ones? Could they ever cancel each other out?
assess.correctAnswer: The first student is right. A Third Law pair is two forces of the SAME type acting on DIFFERENT objects: the table pushes up on the book and the book pushes down on the table. The book's weight (Earth pulling the book) acts on the SAME object as the table's push — the book — so those two are BALANCED forces, not a pair; weight's actual pair is the book pulling the Earth up. To find a pair: state 'A acts on B', and its pair is always 'B acts on A' (same type, different objects).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The table's push up and the book's weight are the Third Law pair — they're equal and opposite.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on naming both objects for every force; a pair must act on two different objects, so weight and the table's push (both on the book) are balanced, not a pair.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the table's push up and the book's weight are the Third Law pair, equal and opposite.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Identifies two forces acting on the SAME object (the book) as a Third Law pair.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The action happens first, then the reaction happens back — there's a tiny delay.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Drop 'action/reaction' language: 'if A pushes B, B pushes A back equally AT THE SAME TIME' — the two forces are simultaneous.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a sequence, a delay, or a 'winner' between the two forces.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The bigger object pushes harder — a truck hits a car, so the truck's force is bigger.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The pair is always equal even for very different masses; the different DAMAGE comes from different accelerations (F = ma), not different forces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the forces in a collision are unequal (the bigger object wins).

responseLevels.gap: Calls any two equal-and-opposite forces a Third Law pair (including two forces on the same object), or describes action-then-reaction with a delay or winner.
responseLevels.full: Identifies pairs by naming 'A on B' and 'B on A' (same type, different objects, simultaneous, equal even for unequal masses), distinguishes them from balanced forces on one object, and applies this to rockets, recoil and collisions.
responseLevels.partial: States the law and gives an example, but can't reliably tell a Third Law pair from balanced forces — names forces without checking that a pair acts on two DIFFERENT objects and is the same type.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A book rests on a table. One student says: 'The table pushing up on the book and the book pushing down on the table are a Newton's Third Law pair.' Another says: 'No — the pair to the table's push up on the book is the book's WEIGHT.' Who is right, and how do you decide which two forces form a Third Law pair?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The classic error is fusing the Third Law pair with balanced forces. Both students name two equal-and-opposite forces, so tier 1 doesn't separate them — the METHOD in tier 2 does. A student who understands N3 checks the two OBJECTS (must differ) and the TYPE (same), correctly rejecting the weight/normal-force option because both act on the book. A student holding the misconception accepts any equal-opposite pair on the same object.
